<div id="n-career" popover class="note">
  <h3>The through-line</h3>
  <p>For fifteen years I ran field-service and distribution operations: a pool service company I owned and operated, and before that a distributor where I was general manager. Those were data jobs before I knew how to write the code: SKU-level demand forecasts, vendor scorecards, technician metrics, route rules and daily KPI dashboards, built in spreadsheets and ERP exports. I made payroll on whether they were right.</p>
  <ul>
    <li><b>Blue Turtle Pool Co.</b>, 2018 to 2026: every job, part, travel leg and incident logged as a dataset, with dashboards for utilization, response time, recurring revenue and churn.</li>
    <li><b>Pool Pros of Hollywood</b>, 2012 to 2022: order, receiving, pick, pack, ship and inventory events in one analytics dataset, with SKU forecasting, reorder rules and vendor scorecards.</li>
  </ul>
  <p>I have never had the luxury of an analysis being interesting but wrong.</p>
  <button class="btn" popovertarget="n-career" popovertargetaction="hide">Close</button>
</div>
<div id="n-results" popover class="note">
  <h3>Where the results come from</h3>
  <ul>
    <li><b>20 percent less travel time</b>: routing and schedule rules, Blue Turtle Pool Co.</li>
    <li><b>30 percent fewer emergency parts buys</b>: inventory and seasonal demand forecasts from service logs, Blue Turtle Pool Co.</li>
    <li><b>25 percent fewer stockouts and rush freight</b>: SKU-level forecasts and automated reorder rules, Pool Pros of Hollywood.</li>
    <li><b>10 percent lower cost of goods</b>: seasonal buys with volume and early-buy discounts, Pool Pros of Hollywood.</li>
  </ul>
  <button class="btn" popovertarget="n-results" popovertargetaction="hide">Close</button>
</div>
<div id="n-training" popover class="note">
  <h3>A plain word on degrees</h3>
  <p>I do not have a CS or statistics degree. My training is self-directed and ongoing: SQL and Machine Learning from IBM, Python from the University of Michigan, Data Analytics and Data Analysis with R Studio from Google, and the Google Analytics certification.</p>
  <p>What I have instead is fifteen years of owning the consequences of an operational number being wrong, and working systems I built and maintain.</p>
  <button class="btn" popovertarget="n-training" popovertargetaction="hide">Close</button>
</div>
<div id="n-pipes" popover class="note">
  <h3>How I build pipelines</h3>
  <p>I build and run a private multi-sport projections platform whose daily pipelines run unattended.</p>
  <p>It runs on rules learned the expensive way: append-only writes, explicit casts on every column, load-timestamped run logs, and calibration checks that fail loudly rather than quietly.</p>
  <button class="btn" popovertarget="n-pipes" popovertargetaction="hide">Close</button>
</div>
<div id="n-model" popover class="note">
  <h3>Where the analysis shows</h3>
  <p>Monte Carlo simulation, XGBoost and CatBoost, Gaussian mixture models for segmentation, Bayesian priors for calibration, and structural causal models when the question is whether a signal is real or only correlated.</p>
  <p>The Broward Airbnb series is the clearest example of the whole loop: raw Inside Airbnb snapshots in R, metrics in SQL, analysis in Python, and a written answer a non-technical investor can act on.</p>
  <a class="btn primary" href="airbnb.html">See the Airbnb case study</a>
  <button class="btn" popovertarget="n-model" popovertargetaction="hide">Close</button>
</div>
